newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia bond ylds up after hostile 24 hours.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia bond ylds up after hostile 24 hours.

text.p: The price action in the Australian bond market in the last 24 hours has led some analysts to believe the rally since September has finally run its course.
While the 10-year bond yield finally made a push below 7.0 percent in afterhours trading, the move met a solid rejection, and coincided with a slide in the Australian dollar.

"I think the way we have been flashing about with 10-year bonds, it really is showing all the hallmarks of a market that's just about gone far enough," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
Today's third quarter GDP, which rose 0.8 percent in the quarter for an annual growth rate of 3.8 percent, brought a fairly mixed response from economists.
Economists at Macquarie bank saw the data providing a solid base for growth in 1996/97, led by business investment in new plant and equipment growth and non-resisential construction.

"With monetary policy now focussed on growth, today's data reduces the chance of another official cut in interest rates - unless the Australian dollar again rises to, and is sustained at, its recent highs," the added in a report.

However, Colonial State Bank saw the report painting a picture of modest growth, falling prices and firm productivity growth, and with the job market outlook remaining weak, it set the pre-conditions for a rate cut.
"Modest economic growth with negligible inflation are ideal conditions for lower bond yields," said Hans Kunnen, Colonial's chief economist.
"Fundamentals are supportive of 10-year bond yields sustainably breaching 7.0 percent to a new trading 6.5 to 7.0 percent," Kunnen added.

Bond yield spreads finished sharply wider to other dollar bloc bonds. The Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread blew out above 100 basis points again, and some analysts feel that the spread narrowing between the two may have finally leveled out.
